newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore hands over British soldiers facing cane.
newsitem.headline: Singapore hands over British soldiers facing cane.

text.p: Two British soldiers charged with robbing a taxi driver in Singapore have been handed over to Britain for prosecution at home, a British High Commission spokesman said on Friday.
A Singapore court agreed on Thursday to transfer the men to British authorities after the prosecution waived its right to exercise jurisdiction, the spokesman told Reuters.
"The transfer to British jurisdiction took place immediately after the court hearing," he said.
The two men, Richard George Britten, 22, and John Thomson King, 20, were turned over to British military authorities and put on a plane to the United Kingdom on Thursday night.

The spokesman gave no further details on where the men would go in Britain or how the prosecution there would proceed. If they had been prosecuted and found guilty in Singapore, the servicemen would have faced at least 12 strokes of the cane and three years in a Singapore jail.
They had been accused of stealing Singapore $43 (US$30).

Although under English law the two men face a maximum penalty of life imprisonment for robbery, such a severe punishment is unlikely given the amount involved, and there is no minimum penalty, British sources said.
The two had been charged with robbing taxi driver Tong Chim Huat, 53, in the early hours of May 3.
Britten is a Royal Marine from Plymouth in southern England, and King is a Royal Engineer from Aberdeenshire, Scotland.

Singapore had originally been expected to deal with the men as if they were Singaporean defendants, but on Thursday a prosecutor told District Judge Vincent Hoong the prosecution was waiving its right to exercise jurisdiction.
The Straits Times on Friday quoted the Singapore attorney-general's chambers as saying the decision to turn the men over to British custody was taken in the public interest.
Singapore has a strict legal system that imposes tough punishments on a range of offences.
Three years ago it faced controversy over the caning of American teenager Michael Fay for vandalism.
His sentence was reduced to four lashes from six after a personal appeal by U.S. President Bill Clinton.

Singapore-style canings are carried out with a rattan cane, a bamboo-like stick that splits the skin and leaves permanent scars, sources familiar with the process said. A doctor is in attendance and checks the person between each stroke. ($1 = S$1.43)
